title: Inside the Traditional Karnataka Home Where Rishab Shetty's Kantara Was Filmed
excerpt: Sai Radha Heritage in Muloor, Udupi, the beachside ancestral home that served as the landlord's residence in the blockbuster film, is now a heritage lodge drawing visitors from across India.
body:
• Sai Radha Heritage in Muloor, Udupi, is the traditional ancestral home where key scenes from Rishab Shetty's Kantara were filmed
  • The nearly 50-year-old beachside property showcases Tulunadu architecture with antique wooden frameworks, carved doors, and vintage furniture
  • Known as "Dhanigala Mane" (the landlord's house) in the film, the property is now a heritage lodge open to visitors and overnight guests

The Landlord's House That Captivated Millions

Long before Kantara became one of Indian cinema's biggest sleeper hits, a heritage home in the coastal village of Muloor, Udupi district, stood quietly by the Arabian Sea. Built nearly five decades ago, Sai Radha Heritage served as the striking backdrop for "Dhanigala Mane" — the landlord's imposing residence that plays a pivotal role in Rishab Shetty's 2022 blockbuster.

The property, which functions as a heritage lodge, has seen a surge in visitor interest since the film's release. Travelers now seek out the home not just for its beachfront location but for the chance to walk through the very rooms and corridors that appeared on screen alongside Shetty, Sapthami Gowda, and Kishore Kumar.

Tulunadu Architecture Brought to Life

What makes the home visually arresting — on screen and in person — is its faithful adherence to traditional Tulunadu architecture. The property features intricately carved wooden frameworks and antique doors sourced from classic coastal Karnataka homes, reassembled to preserve the region's architectural heritage.

According to Indulge Express, the home was "built almost 50 years ago and features the richness of Tulunadu through its architecture and old-style furniture." Rooms blend century-old design sensibilities with modern amenities — antique wooden beds sit alongside air conditioning and contemporary bathrooms, giving guests a taste of heritage without sacrificing comfort.

"Don't forget to visit the Kantara house which is a few meters away. This is where they had shot scenes from the movie."

— TripAdvisor reviewer, April 2023

A Beachside Heritage Experience

Beyond its cinematic connection, Sai Radha Heritage holds its own as a travel destination. The property sits directly on a quiet stretch of beach in the Udupi district, about 32 kilometers from Mangalore's Bajpe Airport. Guests can walk from their rooms to the sand in under a minute.

TripAdvisor reviewers rate the property 4.3 out of 5, with the location earning a near-perfect 4.9 score. Visitors consistently praise the beachfront setting, the spacious rooms with their blend of antique and modern furnishings, and the personalized service model where a dedicated attendant handles all guest needs.

The property operates as a mid-range heritage lodge, making it accessible to travelers who want an immersive cultural experience without luxury hotel pricing.

From Film Set to Cultural Landmark

Kantara's massive success — including the National Award for Best Popular Film Providing Wholesome Entertainment and the Best Actor award for Shetty at the 70th National Film Awards — has turned filming locations across coastal Karnataka into pilgrimage sites for fans.

The Sai Radha Heritage home is part of a broader trend of heritage tourism in the region. Nearby Kundapura, where Shetty grew up and where much of Kantara: Chapter 1 was later filmed across a sprawling 25-acre set, has also seen increased tourist footfall. The sequel, released in October 2025, further amplified interest in the Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts.

Planning a Visit

For travelers looking to experience the property, Sai Radha Heritage is located in Muloor, accessible from both Mangalore and Udupi. The heritage lodge can be found on Google Maps under its name. Visitors recommend combining the stay with exploration of the surrounding coastal Karnataka landscape, including Kundapura's beaches and the region's distinctive temple architecture.

The property serves as a reminder that some of Indian cinema's most evocative settings are not purpose-built sets but real homes carrying decades of history — places where the line between reel and real blurs in the most inviting way.
